title: Buffer Capacity and Choosing a Buffer
short: Pick an acid whose pKa is near the pH you want; more of both parts means more capacity.
trouble: Students think a buffer's capacity depends only on its pH, not on how much acid and base it holds.

blocks.html: A buffer can absorb only so much. From buffer additions you saw that once one partner is used up, the pH changes fast. Two choices decide how well a buffer works: which acid, and how much of it.

Choose a weak acid whose $\text{p}K_a$ is within about 1 unit of the pH you want (ideally close to it). Its capacity, the amount of acid or base it can absorb before the pH shifts a lot, grows with the amounts of HA and $\mathrm{A^-}$ present, and is largest when they are equal.

A buffer works only while both partners are present in useful amounts. At pH = pKa they are equal, so it can absorb acid and base equally well. At $\text{p}K_a \pm 1$, one partner is ten times the other, so the buffer is lopsided. And the pH depends only on the ratio, but how much it can absorb depends on the moles: a 0.01 M buffer and a 1 M buffer can have the same pH, yet the first is used up by 1/100 as much acid.

blocks.name: ch-buffer
blocks.cap: Buffer capacity against pH. It peaks at the pKa and falls off on either side; more of both partners lifts the whole curve.

blocks.title: Choosing a pair
blocks.q: You need a buffer at pH 9.0. Which pair is best: acetic acid/acetate ($\text{p}K_a$ 4.74), $\mathrm{H_2PO_4^-/HPO_4^{2-}}$ (7.21) or $\mathrm{NH_4^+/NH_3}$ (9.25)?

blocks.title: Same pH, different capacity
blocks.q: Two acetate buffers both have pH 4.74: buffer A is $0.010\ \text{M}$ in each partner, buffer B is $0.50\ \text{M}$ in each. To a liter of each, add $0.0050\ \text{mol}$ HCl.
blocks.a: A drops by about half a unit; B barely moves.

blocks.html: Capacity is not unlimited even at its best. A buffer with 0.10 mol of each partner can absorb a little less than 0.10 mol of strong acid before its base is gone, and before that point the pH has already moved a full unit (when the ratio reaches 1 : 10).

items: Use enough acid and base for the amounts you expect to add.
Keep the ratio between about 0.1 and 10.

blocks.html: Thinking a buffer's capacity depends only on its pH. Two buffers at the same pH can differ a hundredfold in how much acid they absorb. Check: compare the moles of each partner with the moles of acid or base you plan to add.
